I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: 'Being looked at sexually' is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision as the index trauma, especially when no other selected items suggest sexual trauma, harassment, or body-focused threat. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Listening for signs that someone is entering the home implies an interpersonal intrusion/assault threat, which does not fit well with a motor vehicle collision and is not supported by the other items. The rest of the threat profile is general hypervigilance to sudden sounds, making this specific home-intruder monitoring item clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
issues.explanation: Avoiding similar clothes usually implies clothing cues tied to the trauma context. For a motor vehicle collision, this is difficult to justify unless other items indicate clothing-specific trauma reminders, which they do not. It also does not connect plausibly to the selected triggers, which are taste, workplace, and sexual objectification.

Workplace as a trigger is weakly grounded for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision given the rest of the profile: the other trigger and threat items are sensory/accident-related, but nothing in appraisals, threat, or strategies explains why the workplace itself would be a salient trauma cue. This makes the trigger set less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste linked to a motor vehicle collision is possible but clinically unusual, and here it is unsupported by memory content or appraisals that would make a gustatory cue understandable. With no memory items and otherwise sound/crash/vehicle-focused content, this trigger stands out as poorly integrated with the formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, a specific taste trigger and an alcohol smell trigger are not impossible, but in combination they imply trauma details (e.g. ingestion, blood, alcohol involvement, hospital/chemical context) that are unsupported by the rest of the profile. The rest of the triggers, threat items, and appraisals are centered on vehicle crash/sound danger, so these sensory triggers look clinically disconnected from the trauma representation described elsewhere.

Undereating as a coping strategy is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links triggers, threat, negative appraisals, and avoidance-based coping around crash-related distress; avoid-driving and screen escape fit that pattern, but food restriction addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, memory, or appraisals. In this profile it appears clinically mismatched rather than a coherent extension of the same trauma-linked cycle.

vignette:
Omar was a man who used to find satisfaction in precision. As a tax inspector, his world was one of numbers, rules, and predictable outcomes. That world ended six months ago at a rain-slicked intersection. He can still feel the sickening jolt of the impact, the screech of metal shearing metal as a dark blue sedan blew through a red light and T-boned his car. The other driver, a young man reeking of whiskey, had stumbled out with a dazed look, but for Omar, the sharp, sweet smell of alcohol became a permanent fixture in his memory, inseparable from the image of shattered glass and his own blood on the dashboard.

In the weeks that followed, the world transformed into a landscape of latent threats. A car backfiring on his street would send him sprawling to the floor, heart hammering against his ribs. He began to operate on a constant, humming frequency of high alert, his body tensed for an impact that never came. This pervasive sense of danger made him scan his environment relentlessly, a habit that paradoxically ensured he was always finding new things to fear. Because he was always watching traffic so closely, he was always spotting dark blue sedans, each one a fresh spark of terror. The sight of any car with a dented fender could send him into a spiral of intrusive images from the crash, his mind replaying the collision with vivid, unwelcome clarity.

These triggers became signals for retreat. After a near-panic attack on the sidewalk when a passing pedestrian’s alcoholic breath washed over him, Omar found himself reaching for his phone. He would lose hours, sometimes entire evenings, scrolling through news feeds or playing repetitive mobile games until his eyes burned. This digital fog was a welcome escape from his own mind. He began avoiding driving entirely, a decision that turned his straightforward commute into a two-hour ordeal on buses and trains, each packed with its own unpredictable sounds and smells. He was also eating less and less; the gnawing emptiness in his stomach felt like one of the few sensations he could still control.

This pattern of avoidance began to carve new, devastating beliefs into his sense of self. Every time he opted for the bus, it was another piece of evidence confirming a verdict he had already passed: *I am no longer capable*. The missed deadlines at work, a direct result of hours lost to his phone, solidified the belief that *I can't rely on myself*. These appraisals were not just thoughts but visceral certainties that poisoned his perception of the world. Because he was so convinced of his own fragility, his hypervigilance intensified; he wasn't just scanning for external dangers anymore, but for signs of his own inevitable failure to cope. This constant self-monitoring made him even more sensitive to potential triggers, turning every similar car from a simple reminder into a direct threat he felt utterly unequipped to handle.

The cycles have now become self-sustaining. The long nights spent staring at a screen leave him exhausted and jittery, amplifying his startle response and making his baseline anxiety even worse. His avoidance of driving has put his job in jeopardy; his manager, once sympathetic, is now speaking of performance reviews and unmet targets. The emotional numbness he feels—the terrifying sense that he will *never be able to feel normal emotions again*—was the final straw in his marriage. His wife left a month ago, telling him it felt like living with a ghost. It is this compounding loss—his job, his marriage, his own sense of competence—that has finally brought him to therapy. Omar sits in the waiting room, a man adrift, terrified that the capable person he once was is gone for good, and hoping, with what little energy he has left, that he is wrong.
